name: Radcore NeutronVeil Reactor Maintenance Suit
description:
A Class-4 radiation suit manufactured for licensed reactor technicians and illegally resold into Shelf black markets where contaminated zones demand it. The outer shell is a pewter-grey woven lead-polymer fabric — heavy, stiff at the shoulders, with a characteristic forward-lean posture after long wear. Dosimeter patches are stitched at the chest and left forearm; most secondhand suits have patches that are faded or missing entirely.

The suit breaks into five modular sections: torso, two arm assemblies, two leg assemblies — all connected by locking ring seals at joints. A thick polycarbonate helmet dome with integrated air filtration scrubber completes the ensemble. New suits smell of antiseptic; old ones smell of nothing, which is somehow worse.
functionality: Rated for gamma and beta radiation shielding. Modular joint seals allow limited limb replacement if a section is compromised. Integrated air scrubber filters particulate and low-level radioactive dust. Dosimeter patches log cumulative exposure. Aug-routing channels run along the outer forearm seams.
what_it_says: You go where the reactors are cracked and someone has to go in first.
worn_by: black-market rad-suit resellers who test product personally
manufacturer: Radcore Systems (corponation licensed); surplus units through Shelf black market
story_hooks: A secondhand suit on the Shelf market still has the original owner's name stenciled inside the collar — that person is listed as missing in a reactor incident three years ago.
Someone is selling counterfeit Radcore suits with substandard lead-polymer content; the dosimeter patches are cosmetic only.
A reactor tech discovers their suit's scrubber was swapped for a non-functional replica — deliberate sabotage, or a supply chain failure?
